title: Toilets when the water is off
summary: Flush with a bucket of water only while the sewer works; if it is broken or backing up, use two buckets, one for pee and one for poo covered with sawdust, and store the bagged waste until it can be got rid of safely.
doFirst: Sewer lines broken, sewage backing up, or told not to flush? Don’t flush. Use the two-bucket toilet below.
Sewer working but the water is off? Flush only when you need to, by pouring a gallon or two of water into the bowl.
Keep pee and poo in separate buckets. Cover each poo with sawdust or shredded paper.
Never pour bleach into a bucket with pee in it.
Wash your hands with soap and water after every toilet visit.

blocks.p: Poop carries germs; pee usually does not. When human waste is not handled properly, flies, pests and rats carry germs from it to food and to the water people drink (Oregon State University Extension). That is how stomach illness spreads through a household or a group.
Use this only while the sewer still works and nothing is backing up. It works for ordinary toilets with a tank, not for toilets with a sealed pressure tank inside (National Park Service).

steps: Pour a gallon or two (4 to 8 L) of water into the bowl. The amount varies by toilet (National Park Service; DC Water says a gallon).
Pour slowly at first, then fast, to make it flush. Avoid splashing (DC Water, National Park Service).
If the water rises without draining, stop (National Park Service).
If needed, slowly add a little water to bring the bowl back to its usual level. Don’t use the handle as well (National Park Service).

list: Water you would not drink is fine for flushing. New York State Department of Health: “There is no need to disinfect water used for flushing.”
Keep grease, food scraps, wipes and cleaning chemicals out of the flushing water (National Park Service).
Save water: you can use the toilet several times for pee before you flush (DC Water).

Sewer or water lines are broken. After an earthquake, flood or similar damage, don’t flush until officials say it is OK (Jefferson and Clallam County emergency management). The pipes in your house may be fine while the pipes in the street are broken (Oregon State University Extension).
The toilet does not drain normally, or sewage comes back up (National Park Service). Stop using it.
Your septic system is flooded, or the soil around it is (New York State Department of Health). See Septic systems below.

blocks.p: If you hear of broken water or sewer lines, also shut the main water valve to keep dirty water out of your pipes (FEMA).
Then use the two-bucket toilet, or line the toilet bowl with bags.

This is what Oregon and Washington emergency managers and Oregon State University Extension tell households to set up. Keeping pee and poo apart matters: pee mixed with poo is what makes a toilet smell (Oregon State University Extension).

steps: Get two 5-gallon (19 L) buckets with lids. Mark one “pee” and one “poo” (Oregon State University Extension).
Line the poo bucket with a heavy-duty 13-gallon (49 L) garbage bag. The pee bucket needs no liner (Oregon State University Extension).

Put the buckets in a private place, with cover material and a scoop nearby (Jefferson County). Cover material: sawdust, wood shavings, shredded paper, bark chips or peat moss (Oregon State University Extension).
Move the toilet seat to whichever bucket you are using. After use, take the seat off and put a lid on that closes well (Jefferson and Clallam County).
Pee in the pee bucket. Put the toilet paper in the poo bucket (Washington County, Oregon).
Try not to pee in the poo bucket (Oregon State University Extension). Mistakes happen; do your best (Jefferson County).

After each poo, sprinkle about half a cup (120 mL) of cover material so it covers the poo completely (Oregon State University Extension). It soaks up moisture, cuts smell and keeps flies off (Wilsonville, Oregon).

blocks.p: Diapers, sanitary pads and bagged pet waste don’t go in either bucket (Jefferson County). See Garbage and dirty water.

steps: Pee bucket: empty it when it is about a quarter full, or before it gets too heavy to carry safely (Oregon State University Extension).

Add water you would not drink, if you have it, to dilute the pee, and pour it on the lawn or bare ground (Washington County, Oregon State University Extension). Pick a different spot each time (Oregon State University Extension). Keep it well away from any well, spring or stream.
Poo bucket: fill it no more than half full (Oregon State University Extension, Washington County).
Put on disposable gloves. Tie the bag shut, put it in a second bag and seal that too (Oregon State University Extension).
Line the bucket with a new bag (Oregon State University Extension).
Take off the gloves and wash your hands.

blocks.p: If officials have told you to hold everything, keep the pee in a bucket with a tight lid too, and wait for their instructions (Jefferson and Clallam County).
If you only have the toilet itself, use it as the seat.

steps: Shut off the water valve to the toilet and get the water out of the bowl (North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services).
Line the bowl, or a bucket, with two heavy-duty plastic garbage bags (King County public health).
Put cat litter, fireplace ashes or sawdust in the bottom of the bags (King County).
At the end of each day, tie the bags securely and move them to a protected place such as a garage, basement or outbuilding until there is a safe way to get rid of them (King County).

blocks.warn: Never pour bleach into a bucket or bag that has pee in it. Pee contains ammonia, and bleach mixed with ammonia makes toxic chloramine gas (Washington State Department of Health). Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner (CDC).

blocks.p: The two-bucket agencies use cover material, not chemicals. Some older guides say to add bleach or disinfectant to a single toilet bucket; this app does not.
Wear gloves. Empty the bucket first. North Carolina’s health department says to disinfect a waste bucket with bleach or throw it away.
CDC’s bleach mix for household items: 1 cup (240 mL) of plain, unscented household bleach (5% to 9%) in 5 gallons (19 L) of water. Let the bucket air dry. Indoors, open windows and doors (CDC).

list: Keep the double-bagged poo in a separate garbage can with a tight lid, apart from other garbage (Oregon State University Extension; Anchorage emergency management).
Keep it far from food and water, out of reach of children, pets, flies and rats (Oregon State University Extension, Washington County).
A garage, basement or outbuilding works (King County).
Don’t put human waste in the normal garbage (Oregon State University Extension), unless officials announce that you may (King County).

blocks.p: You will likely have to store the waste until the public sewer is fixed (Oregon State University Extension). Listen for instructions from officials and the garbage haulers (Washington County).

list: Into a working sewer or septic system, once it works again (King County).

Bury it on your own land (King County), but never within 100 feet (30 m) of a water source or where it can seep downhill into one (Oregon State University Extension). This app uses the more cautious 200 feet (60 m): see Latrines and cat holes.
In town, don’t dig pits: germs spread easily to neighboring properties (Jefferson County). King County says latrines are not right for urban places.
Never wash waste into a storm drain (Salt Lake County Health Department) or put it in a ditch or stream.
A septic tank that drains to the leach field by gravity keeps working with the power off (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension). You can flush it with a bucket as above.

If your system has a pump, an aerobic unit or a sand filter, it needs electricity. Without power, waste collects in the system. For a short outage, use water only for flushing and hand washing. If the power will be out a long time, stop all water use (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension), and use the bucket toilet.
Stop all water use if the plumbing starts to drain slowly (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension).
Don’t use the system if the soil around it is flooded (New York State Department of Health, EPA). Don’t pump the tank while the ground is flooded (EPA).
Signs of damage: slow plumbing, sewage backing up, the ground settling or washing out around the leach field (New York State Department of Health, EPA).
After an earthquake, don’t assume the system works even if you have power and water (Clallam County).
If you will later empty the poo bucket into your own septic tank, don’t add cover material to it: it can’t go in a septic system (Clallam County).

blocks.p: Wash with soap and water after every toilet visit and before eating (Washington County). Hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol will do when there is no water, but soap and water clean best (Oregon State University Extension; Wilsonville, Oregon).

sources.name: Jefferson County Department of Emergency Management with Clallam County Sheriff’s Emergency Management, Twin-Bucket Emergency Toilet, sanitary sewer version (updated March 2015)
sources.used: Do not flush until a local official says it is OK; private space with carbon material and a scoop; seat moved between buckets, lid that closes well; try not to mix, mistakes happen; toilet paper in the poo bucket; urine has almost no health risk; store and wait for disposal instructions; no diapers, pads or pet waste in the buckets; do not dig a pit privy, disease spreads to neighboring properties

sources.name: Clallam County Environmental Health and Emergency Management, Twin-Bucket Emergency Toilet, septic system version (updated March 2015)
sources.used: Some septic systems need electricity for a pump; after an earthquake do not assume the septic system works; store pee and poo with tight lids and wait for instructions; no carbon material in a poo bucket that will be emptied into a septic tank

sources.name: Washington County, Oregon, Emergency Management (Take5), Disaster Sanitation
sources.used: Line poo bucket with a heavy-duty 13-gallon bag; cover each use with carbon material; no more than half full; double-bag, store away from food and water, secure from pets, flies and rats; toilet paper in the poo bucket; add non-drinking water to pee, pour on lawn, garden or ground; listen to waste haulers; clean hands after toileting and before eating

sources.name: City of Wilsonville, Oregon, The Two-Bucket Toilet Solution (credits the Regional Disaster Preparedness Organization)
sources.used: Cover material absorbs moisture, reduces odor and deters flies; urine usually sterile, poop carries pathogens; soap and water clean better than hand sanitizer

sources.name: National Park Service, Grand Canyon, How to Flush a Toilet with a Bucket (October 13, 2026)
sources.used: A gallon or two, varies by toilet; pour steadily then faster; avoid splashes; stop if the water rises without draining; restore the standing level, do not also use the handle; gravity toilets only, not sealed pressure vessels; no grease, food scraps, wipes or cleaning chemicals; stop using a toilet that does not drain normally

sources.name: DC Water, What’s on Tap, Preparedness Issue (2021)
sources.used: A gallon of water poured into the bowl, slowly then quickly; several uses for liquid waste before flushing

sources.name: New York State Department of Health, Boil Water Notices: Frequently Asked Questions for Residents and Homeowners (question 24)
sources.used: “There is no need to disinfect water used for flushing.”

sources.name: FEMA, American Red Cross and USDA, Food and Water in an Emergency
sources.used: Shut the incoming water valve if you hear of broken water or sewage lines

sources.name: North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, Toilet Use During an Emergency (October 2024)
sources.used: Turn off the water valve and flush out the water in the bowl before lining it; disinfect the bucket with bleach or discard it

sources.name: Public Health – Seattle & King County, How to create an emergency toilet
sources.used: Line the bowl or a pail with two heavy-duty bags; cat litter, fireplace ashes or sawdust in the bottom; tie and remove daily to a garage, basement or outbuilding; dispose into a working sewer or septic system or bury on your own property; bags in regular garbage only if officials announce it; latrines not appropriate in urban locations

sources.name: Municipality of Anchorage Office of Emergency Management, Sanitation and Hygiene in an Emergency
sources.used: Large garbage can with heavy liner and tight-fitting lid for bagged waste (its 1 cup bleach to 10 cups water disinfectant, with no bleach strength, is not used)

sources.name: Washington State Department of Health, Dangers of Mixing Bleach with Cleaners
sources.used: Ammonia is found in urine; caution with diaper pails and toilet bowls; bleach and ammonia make toxic chloramine gases

sources.name: CDC, How to Safely Clean and Sanitize with Bleach (reviewed August 26, 2026)
sources.used: Plain unscented bleach 5% to 9%; 1 cup (240 mL) of bleach to 5 gallons of water for non-food household surfaces and items; air dry; open windows and doors indoors; never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner

sources.name: Salt Lake County Health Department, Cleaning Up Bodily Fluids and Human Waste
sources.used: Never wash waste into a storm drain

sources.name: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, Onsite Wastewater Treatment Systems: Responding to Electrical Power Outages and Floods (ER-001)
sources.used: Gravity septic systems keep working in an outage; systems with electrical parts (aerobic units, sand filters) collect wastewater; short outage: water only for flushing and hand washing; extended outage: stop all water use; stop if plumbing drains slowly

sources.name: US EPA, Septic Systems: What to Do after the Flood (updated August 24, 2026)
sources.used: Don’t use the system while the soil is saturated and flooded; don’t pump the tank in flooded conditions; signs of damage: settling, can’t accept water

sources.name: New York State Department of Health, Trash Disposal and Septic Systems after Weather Emergencies (revised October 2023)
sources.used: Don’t use the septic system if the soil around it is flooded; signs of damage: sluggish plumbing, sewage backup, erosion around the drain field
